# Preface {.unnumbered}

This is a short book about one confusion in gridded data, and about the
communities and software that keep it alive.

People say a grid is "curvilinear" when they mean several different things:
that its coordinates are stored as two-dimensional longitude and latitude
arrays, that it is in geographic coordinates at all, or that its cells
really do follow curved lines that no simple formula can describe. Those
are different claims. Treating them as one leads to files that are larger than they need to be, to coordinates
that are less precise than the numbers they replaced, to software that
refuses a perfectly regular grid, and to analysis that resamples data that
never needed resampling.

## The stance

The book takes one position and argues it throughout:

> **A grid is not regular, rectilinear or curvilinear on its own. It is
> regular, rectilinear or curvilinear *in a frame*.**

"What kind of grid is this?" is really two questions. How is each cell's
position worked out from its row and column? And in which coordinate frame
are those positions written down? The second question changes the answer to
the first. The NSIDC 25 km sea ice grid is regular in its polar
stereographic frame and curvilinear in longitude and latitude. A
rotated-pole climate model grid is regular in rotated longitude and latitude
and curvilinear in true longitude and latitude. Neither grid changed; only
the frame did.

So when this book says "regular", it always means "regular in some named
frame", and the most useful question to ask of any dataset is the title:
*regular in what?*

## Who this is for

Gridded data is shared between communities that learned to think about it
in different ways. Remote sensing and GIS treat an affine transform as the
truth and everything else as something to be warped away. Climate and ocean
modelling treat coordinate arrays as the complete description of a grid.
Array computing treats dimensions as axes and coordinates as labels.
Scientific visualisation classifies grids by how much must be stored, and
has no coordinate reference system at all. Each view is right for the work
it grew up doing. The trouble happens where they meet.

This book is for people who meet that boundary: a modeller whose output has
to work in GIS tools, a remote sensing analyst handed a netCDF file, a
software developer writing a reader, a data producer deciding how to store
coordinates. It does not assume you belong to any one of those camps, and
it tries to explain each one in its own terms before comparing them.

## How to read it

- Part I (chapters 1 to 3) sets out the idea: the problem, the two
  questions, and the many ways one grid can be stored.
- Part II (chapters 4 and 5) puts the communities and their software side by
  side on the same data.
- Part III (chapters 6 to 8) is for working with real files: a field guide,
  worked cases, and where the whole framework stops applying.

If you arrived with an objection, such as "Wikipedia already defines a
regular grid", @sec-misreadings collects the common ones with short
answers.

Code is shown in R and Python, and in GDAL command line form where that is
simplest. It is not run when the book is built. The figures are built from
published grid specifications by `scripts/make_figures.py`, and the numbers
quoted alongside them come from that script.

## Where this comes from

The material here was consolidated from blog posts on hypertidy.org
(2022 to 2026), working notes in the gdal-r-python repository, two earlier
book drafts (rw-book and a-book), the trianglewins notes on dimension, and
several long working conversations. The source map is in `README.md`.
